# Sources: geography topic discovery (niche "geography", about 10 minutes, English)

One entry per source. "Access" says how much of it was actually read: read (the text itself, or the part that matters), indirect (only through another source), snippet (only a search summary: a lead, never a source).

### S1. Terence McCarthy and Marc Humphries (University of the Witwatersrand), "Comment on 'Highly Contrasted Geochemical Pattern in Sediments of the Okavango Delta, Botswana Driven by Dust Supply, Hydrological Heritage and Biogeochemical Reactions' by Jolivet et al.", Geochemistry, Geophysics, Geosystems 25, e2023GC011165 (AGU / Wiley, open access), 2024 (accepted 19 November 2023)
- Secondary: a peer-reviewed comment in which the island model's originators summarise their own primary field studies (1986-2012: 18 islands, about 200 auger holes, about a thousand soil samples) and rebut a rival model. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1029/2023GC011165 . Copy read: https://wiredspace.wits.ac.za/bitstreams/33c54c62-5465-42c7-8335-3de2e9686157/download (handle 10539/40814)
- Access: read (the whole six-page text, extracted from the repository PDF; the figures could not be viewed)
- Supports: C01, C03, C04, C05, C06, C07, C08, C09, C10, C11, C12, C13, C14, C17. Counterevidence: Jolivet et al. 2023 (S6) and Challier et al. 2026 (S2) dispute how the island groundwater's chemistry forms (C12). S3 gives "less than 1%" leaving at the southern outlet where S1 gives "about 2%" leaving as surface flow (C01): two measures, same order.
- Status: expert and current (2024) on the delta's hydrology and the island model; on the dispute it speaks for one side. Its statement that independent groups tested the model (Bauer et al. 2006, geophysical imaging; Bauer-Gottwein et al. 2007, modelling) is a citation I did not read. The per-year unit of the 380,000-tonne solute figure is implied by the sentences either side of it ("each year"), not stated in that sentence.

### S2. Valentin Challier, Marc Jolivet (IPGP, Université Paris Cité, CNRS), Nashaat Mazrui (Okavango Research Institute, University of Botswana), Aline Dia, Mélanie Davranche, Olivier Dauteuil, Maxime Pattier, Patrice Petitjean, Lionel Dutruch (Géosciences Rennes, CNRS), "Beyond Expectations: Unusual Water and Salt Chemistry in the Okavango Delta (Botswana)", EGU General Assembly 2026, abstract EGU26-12221 (session HS10.12), 2026
- Primary: a conference abstract reporting new major- and trace-element analyses of the islands' salt deposits, compared with the Makgadikgadi pans' evaporites (not peer-reviewed). URL: https://meetingorganizer.copernicus.org/EGU26/EGU26-12221.html
- Access: read (the abstract, through the fetch tool's account of it with short verbatim excerpts; not the full wording)
- Supports: C06 (the island salts are "essentially trona"; saline, alkaline groundwater beneath), C12 (the groundwater composition "could not result from a simple evapotranspiration of surface water"; added "(bio)geochemical processes" proposed), C17 (the Makgadikgadi evaporites are mostly halite). Counterevidence: S1 rejects the predecessor two-aquifer model (Jolivet et al. 2023, S6) as resting on insufficient data.
- Status: the newest work found (2026), from a group independent of S1 that includes the delta's own research institute; unreviewed. It calls the evapotranspiration model incomplete, not wrong.

### S3. Diana Chavarro-Rincon (Princeton University), Piotr Wolski and Mike Murray-Hudson (Okavango Research Institute, University of Botswana), Kelly Caylor (Princeton University), "The role of vegetation dynamics in the small-scale water balance of the Okavango Delta", Geophysical Research Abstracts 13, EGU2011-13435, EGU General Assembly 2011
- Primary: a conference abstract on sap-flow measurements on Nxaraga island; its background states the delta's flood timing and its 37-year water balance. URL: https://meetingorganizer.copernicus.org/EGU2011/EGU2011-13435.pdf
- Access: read (the whole one-page abstract, text extracted from the PDF)
- Supports: C01 ("less than 1% of the inflow leaves the Delta in the southern outlet", from "hydrological data of the last 37 years"), C02 (the flood "arrives during the dry season, long after the end of rains (3 to 4 months)", moving "very slowly through this low gradient system"), C03 ("a tropical freshwater wetland complex"), C08 (in part: water inside the islands "is transpired by woody vegetation", stated conditionally), C16 (flooded area "12,000 km2 (average years) to 15,000 km2 (extremely wet years)"). Counterevidence: S1's "about 2%" (a different measure).
- Status: hydrologists of the delta's own research institute, independent of S1's group. 2011 and an abstract: the water-balance and timing figures are background from records, not new measurements. Nothing found replaces them.

### S4. NASA Earth Observatory (caption by Michon Scott; image by Jesse Allen and Robert Simmon from EO-1 ALI data), "Not Your Usual Flooding in Botswana", Image of the Day, 5 June 2012
- Popular: a science agency's image caption quoting Frank Eckardt (University of Cape Town) and Guido van Langenhove (Hydrological Services Namibia). URL: https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-observatory/not-your-usual-flooding-in-botswana-78166/
- Access: read (the whole caption)
- Supports: C02 (rains "over Angola from October through March" do not usually "reach the bottom of the Okavango Delta until July"; an "extremely shallow gradient"), C13 ("some of these depressions only fill with water after decades of dryness"), C15 ("the rains fall in the Angolan Highlands and travel about 450 kilometers"). Counterevidence: 2012 itself was the exception the caption is about: the water came early and overflowed into the Savuti River.
- Status: a credible popular account from 2012, agreeing with S3 on the timing. It does not mention faults, islands or salt.

### S5. Lars Ramberg and Piotr Wolski (Okavango Research Institute), "Growing islands and sinking solutes: processes maintaining the endorheic Okavango Delta as a freshwater system", Plant Ecology 196(2): 215-231 (Springer), 2008
- Secondary: a peer-reviewed synthesis with its own budget calculations. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1007/s11258-007-9346-1
- Access: snippet (a search summary of the abstract only; the publisher page redirected to an authorisation step that was not followed, and the Semantic Scholar record carries no abstract)
- Supports (as a lead only): C01 (98-99% of the water lost to evapotranspiration), C04 (94% of inflowing solutes retained), C08 (islands as the main solute sink). Also gives about 150,000 islands in 13,500 km2 and an island complex 100,000-400,000 years old, used nowhere here. Counterevidence: none seen.
- Status: not read, so it supports nothing on its own. Its 94% may rest on the same measurements as S1, so it would not be independent on C04. Read it before any line uses the island count or the ages.

### S6. Marc Jolivet, Olivier Dauteuil, Aline Dia, Mélanie Davranche, Anne-Catherine Pierson-Wickmann, Laurie Barrier et al., "Highly contrasted geochemical pattern in sediments of the Okavango Delta, Botswana driven by dust supply, hydrological heritage and biogeochemical reactions", Geochemistry, Geophysics, Geosystems 24(6), e2023GC010978, 2023
- Primary: the study proposing two disconnected aquifers beneath the delta, from six auger holes on Nxaraga Island. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1029/2023GC010978
- Access: indirect (known only through its critics' account in S1 and its successors' summary in S2)
- Supports: C12 (one side of the dispute). Counterevidence: S1.
- Status: not read. Its own words should be read before the film describes its argument.

### S7. Authors and title not seen (a study of where the delta's inflow originates), Environmental Monitoring and Assessment (Springer), 2023
- Primary: a hydrological study. URL: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10661-023-11448-7
- Access: snippet (search summary only)
- Supports (as a lead only): C15 (over 95% of the inflow originates as rain on the Angolan Highlands). Counterevidence: none seen.
- Status: not read.

### S8. Maya F. Stokes, Samuel L. Goldberg, J. Taylor Perron (MIT), "Ongoing River Capture in the Amazon", Geophysical Research Letters 45(11): 5545-5552, 2018
- Primary: the peer-reviewed study. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1029/2018GL078129
- Access: snippet (search summaries of its abstract and of press coverage; the paper was not opened, and the AGU blog post about it now returns 404)
- Supports (as a lead): C18, C19, and T2's M3 (headward incision by a fast-eroding Rio Negro tributary, sedimentation in the Orinoco below the fork, seasonal flooding of a low divide, a positive feedback; an "unstable bifurcation" likely to end in full capture). Counterevidence: none seen.
- Status: not read.

### S9. Pesquisa FAPESP (author not named), "Continuous expansion of the Amazon River", Pesquisa FAPESP issue 271, September 2018
- Popular: a science magazine's report of S8. URL: https://revistapesquisa.fapesp.br/en/continuous-expansion-of-the-amazon-river/
- Access: read (the whole article)
- Supports: C18 (the Casiquiare "diverts about a quarter of its waters to the Rio Negro"), C19 (its flow "will continue to increase"; in "the distant future" all upper-Orinoco water; the Amazon basin could grow by "up to 40,000 square kilometers"), C20 (signs that several west-bank Amazon tributaries were captured from the Orinoco basin). Counterevidence: none.
- Status: a credible popular report of one study, 2018. It gives no mechanism and no timescale.

### S10. Authors and title not seen, Water 11(10): 2068 (MDPI), 2019
- Secondary: a hydrology paper with historical background. URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4441/11/10/2068/htm
- Access: snippet
- Supports (as a lead): T2's M4 (Humboldt and Bonpland navigated the Casiquiare on 10 May 1800 and "closed the controversy" over whether the Amazon and the Orinoco were connected). Counterevidence: none seen.
- Status: not read.

### S11. Author not seen, a text on Humboldt's Orinoco journey and Buache's maps, Archive ouverte UNIGE (University of Geneva), date not seen
- Secondary (scholarly). URL: https://access.archive-ouverte.unige.ch/access/metadata/b733953d-82ae-427b-8547-a57912fd6414/download
- Access: snippet
- Supports (as a lead): T2's M4 (Buache's maps placed a mountain range between the two basins; Humboldt looked for it on the ground). Counterevidence: the same summary says Humboldt was confident of the connection before he set out.
- Status: not read.

### S12. Hongbin Yu (NASA Goddard / University of Maryland) et al., "The fertilizing role of African dust in the Amazon rainforest: a first multiyear assessment based on CALIPSO lidar observations" (title as listed in the search results, not checked against the paper), Geophysical Research Letters, 2015
- Primary: a peer-reviewed study using CALIOP lidar data, 2007-2013. URL: https://acd-ext.gsfc.nasa.gov/People/Chin/papers/Yu_grl_2015.pdf
- Access: snippet
- Supports (as a lead): T3's M1 and M2 (28 (8-48) Tg of dust a year reaching the Amazon basin; 0.022 (0.006-0.037) Tg of phosphorus a year, which the authors call comparable to the basin's hydrological loss). Counterevidence: the wide ranges are the study's own.
- Status: not read.

### S13. University of Maryland, Department of Astronomy news, "Massive Amounts of Saharan Dust Fertilize the Amazon Rainforest", 2015 (date implied by the study it reports)
- Popular: a university press release about S12. URL: https://www.astro.umd.edu/news-events/news/massive-amounts-saharan-dust-fertilize-amazon-rainforest
- Access: snippet
- Supports (as a lead): T3's M1 (27.7 million tons a year) and M3 (the Bodélé Depression, an ancient lake bed with deposits of dead microorganisms rich in phosphorus). Counterevidence: none seen.
- Status: not read; a press release's framing.
